ai-at-work.title: Uber caps employee AI spending after blowing through budget in four months
ai-at-work.excerpt: Uber's cutback has occurred after the company had reportedly encouraged staff to use AI as much as possible.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Uber told employees to go wild with AI tools, burned through their entire annual budget in four months, and now they're capping spending like they just got the credit card bill. This matters because it's a real-world reminder that "move fast and break things" doesn't work when the thing you're breaking is your budget, and it shows how quickly AI enthusiasm can outpace actual planning. The irony is delicious: a company that disrupted entire industries apparently didn't think to, you know, budget for the disruption they were creating internally.

ai-at-work.title: New Microsoft tool lets devs spin up AI behavior tests using text descriptions
ai-at-work.excerpt: Microsoft on Tuesday took the wraps off Adaptive Spec-driven Scoring for Evaluation and Regression Testing, an open source framework for spinning up AI evaluations.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Microsoft released an open source framework called Adaptive Spec-driven Scoring for Evaluation and Regression Testing that lets developers test AI behavior using simple text descriptions instead of writing complex evaluation code. This matters because it could speed up how quickly teams deploy AI features to their digital workplaces, which means fewer delays between "we built this" and "people can actually use it." Honestly, if this tool does what it claims, it might finally give us a break from the endless cycle of AI projects that sound amazing in demos but arrive at work broken and confused about basic instructions.

ai-at-work.title: Martin Scorsese becomes the latest — and most unlikely — Hollywood voice for AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: The caveat is that one of the world's most famous living directors is using the tech solely for storyboarding.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Martin Scorsese is using AI tools to help with storyboarding for his films, marking an unexpected endorsement from one of cinema's most celebrated directors. For digital workplace professionals, this matters because it shows even the most traditionally minded creatives are finding practical, limited applications for AI rather than wholesale transformation. Here's the thing though: Scorsese using AI for storyboards is basically the workplace equivalent of your skeptical boss finally admitting Slack saves time. It's not revolutionary, it's just pragmatic, and honestly that's the healthiest AI adoption story we're hearing.

ai-at-work.title: Microsoft launches Scout, an OpenClaw-inspired personal assistant
ai-at-work.excerpt: Launched at Build, Microsoft Scout is a new AI assistant meant to bring the power and flexibility of OpenClaw into the Microsoft 365 system.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Microsoft just dropped Scout, an AI assistant designed to integrate OpenClaw's capabilities into the Microsoft 365 ecosystem. This matters because digital workplace leaders are drowning in fragmented tools and half-baked AI features, so anything that actually ties things together gets attention. Look, I've seen Microsoft launch assistants before, and I'll believe this one moves the needle when I see actual adoption numbers instead of just impressive demo videos at Build.

tools-tech.title: AI Model Release Tracker: Microsoft AI's first reasoning model arrives
tools-tech.excerpt: Not every new model is all it's cracked up to be. Our tracker keeps each release in context with its peers, so you know which models are worth your time.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft released its first reasoning model, and ZDNet created a tracker to help people sort through the noise of AI model launches. For digital workplace folks, this matters because reasoning models could actually handle complex document workflows and decision-making tasks instead of just spitting out marketing copy. Here's the thing though: half the models that land with fanfare in January are forgotten by April, so until this thing proves itself in actual office environments, I'm keeping my champagne corked.

tools-tech.title: Build 2026: Microsoft's MDASH exits preview with 100+ specialized threat-hunting AI agents
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft's Build 2026 security news centers on an agentic AI vulnerability system designed to find real exploitable flaws, connect them to Defender and GitHub, and help developers fix them faster.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft rolled out MDASH from preview with over 100 AI agents that hunt for actual exploitable vulnerabilities and wire them directly into Defender and GitHub so developers can fix them faster. This matters because most digital workplaces are drowning in security alerts while real threats slip through the noise, and having AI that separates signal from actual risk could actually make security teams functional instead of buried. The irony is we finally have AI agents doing something genuinely useful instead of writing mediocre emails, which means security teams might finally get their afternoon back.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft's first reasoning model is one of 7 AIs just released at Build - what we know so far
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft AI has fully joined the conversation with MAI-Thinking-1, alongside new coding, image, and voice models.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft dropped seven new AI models at Build, including MAI-Thinking-1, their answer to reasoning-focused AI that can actually work through problems step by step instead of just pattern matching. This matters because digital workplace teams are about to get pestered by every vendor claiming their tool now has "reasoning AI" built in, which means separating real capability from marketing noise just got harder. After three decades watching tech cycles, I'll believe the reasoning claims when I see them actually help knowledge workers solve real problems instead of just generating longer, more confident-sounding wrong answers.

tools-tech.title: Work IQ is Microsoft's big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft's Work IQ could make enterprise AI agents dramatically smarter, but the shift to agent-first IT brings serious questions about cost, governance, data exposure, and operational risk.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft launched Work IQ, positioning AI agents as the primary interface for enterprise IT rather than humans using tools. This matters because if agent-first systems become standard, digital workplace pros need to understand how their governance, security, and cost models completely flip on their head. Honestly, I'm with ZDNet on the skepticism here: we've seen plenty of enterprise AI bets that looked revolutionary until they hit the messy reality of actual data, actual compliance, and actual budget spreadsheets.

digital-culture.title: What if it’s us who can learn something from Gen Z about work?
digital-culture.excerpt: If there were ever a truth about generationalism, it’s this: Every generation has the same complaint about the generation that came after it. Kids these days don’t want to work. They want everything b
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company is arguing that older generations might actually have something to learn from Gen Z about work attitudes rather than the usual complaint cycle going the other way. This matters because if your digital workplace strategy is built on outdated assumptions about motivation, loyalty, and what people want from their jobs, you're going to keep missing talent and engagement opportunities. Here's the thing: Gen Z didn't invent the idea that work should have meaning and boundaries, they just had the audacity to say it out loud instead of suffering quietly like we did.

digital-culture.title: A guide to navigating uncertainty head-on
digital-culture.excerpt: Below, Simone Stolzoff shares five key insights from his new book, How to Not Know: The Value of Uncertainty in a World That Demands Answers. Simone is a journalist. His work has been featured in The
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece on Simone Stolzoff's book about embracing uncertainty rather than fighting it. This matters because digital workplace leaders spend half their time trying to predict what remote work will look like next year, which tools will stick around, and whether AI will replace their job by Tuesday. Here's the thing: you can't control any of that, but you can control whether your team drowns in analysis paralysis or actually ships something meaningful while you wait for clarity.

digital-culture.title: AI has an unexpected side effect: It could make high-paying jobs less hostile to women
digital-culture.excerpt: The conversation about AI and work revolves mostly around jobs being destroyed or new ones emerging, around the workers benefiting and those likely to be left behind. All these debates are legitimate.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Microsoft and other tech companies are discovering that AI tools might accidentally reduce workplace hostility toward women by removing some human bias from decision-making processes. This matters to digital workplace leaders because it suggests AI implementation could have unexpected benefits beyond efficiency gains, potentially improving retention and psychological safety for underrepresented groups. Of course, we should probably fix the sexism directly instead of waiting for an algorithm to do it for us, but I'll take wins wherever I find them.

digital-culture.title: Why smart leaders lose it during meetings
digital-culture.excerpt: High-pressure situations at work, like an important meeting, are often the backdrop for our most reactive professional moments. In 2025 nearly two-thirds (60%) of employees who spent more than 15 hour
digital-culture.dwp_take: A new study found that 60 percent of employees stuck in more than 15 hours of meetings weekly report severe stress, and that high-pressure situations trigger reactive rather than thoughtful responses. For digital workplace leaders, this is a wake-up call that endless meetings aren't just annoying, they're actively degrading decision-making quality and psychological safety across teams. If your leadership team is spending more time in video calls than actually thinking, you've built a stress machine, not a workplace.

industry-news.title: Fake Claude Code Installers Deliver Credential-Stealing Malware
industry-news.excerpt: Fake Claude Code install sites are pushing malware that steals API keys, developer credentials, crypto wallets, and other sensitive data. The post Fake Claude Code Installers Deliver Credential-Steali
industry-news.dwp_take: Cybercriminals have set up fake installation sites for Claude Code that deliver malware designed to steal API keys, developer credentials, and crypto wallets from unsuspecting users. This matters because your developers and knowledge workers are exactly the targets here, and a compromised credential can turn your entire systems into an open door for attackers. Here's the thing: we've been saying for years that people will click anything if it looks official, and apparently 30 years of IT security theater hasn't changed human behavior one bit.

industry-news.title: Google Patches Android Zero-Day Vulnerability in June 2026 Security Update
industry-news.excerpt: Google’s June 2026 Android update fixes dozens of flaws, including a potentially exploited Framework vulnerability and critical system bugs. The post Google Patches Android Zero-Day Vulnerability in J
industry-news.dwp_take: Google released its June 2026 Android security update, which addresses multiple vulnerabilities including a zero-day flaw in the Android Framework that may have already been exploited. For digital workplace teams, this matters because plenty of your workforce still relies on Android devices for email, VPNs, and accessing company systems, so unpatched devices create real security risks. Here's the thing though: most organizations will probably wait three months to deploy this while their MDM team argues about testing timelines, which is exactly how breaches happen.

industry-news.title: SpaceX IPO Filing Ties AI Growth to Water Access
industry-news.excerpt: SpaceX’s amended IPO filing adds water access to the risks around its AI data center buildout, putting another physical constraint around its growth plans. The post SpaceX IPO Filing Ties AI Growth to
industry-news.dwp_take: SpaceX disclosed in its IPO filing that water availability is a material risk factor for expanding its AI data center operations. This matters because it highlights how digital infrastructure isn't just about servers and code anymore—physical resources like water are now business-critical bottlenecks that affect scaling timelines and location decisions. Turns out you can't run a modern AI operation on hopes and venture capital alone, which is refreshing honesty from a company usually selling us futures that ignore earthly constraints.

industry-news.title: Microsoft Teams File Outage Resolved, but IT Teams Still Need to Check Fallbacks
industry-news.excerpt: Microsoft restored Teams and Office for the web file access after a June 1 outage, but the root cause remained unclear. IT teams should verify tenant impact and fallback paths. The post Microsoft Team
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft Teams went down on June 1 and knocked out file access for users, but they got things running again without ever really explaining what broke. This matters because if your entire organization depends on Teams for daily work, an unexplained outage means you have no real assurance it won't happen the same way tomorrow. Here's my take: "root cause remains unclear" is corporate speak for "we have no idea," and that should terrify every IT leader who's been told to consolidate everything into one cloud platform.
